Typical wording: Agreement automatically renews for successive one-year terms unless written notice of termination is provided at least sixty (60) days prior to the end of the then-current term
What it means: Contract auto-renews indefinitely for 1-year periods. If you don't send a cancellation notice 60 days before each renewal, you're locked in for another year.
Negotiating position: Ask for 30-day notice instead of 60. If vendor refuses, ask for annual price-change notice at the 90-day mark so you have time to evaluate alternatives.

Typical wording: Fees for any renewal term shall not increase by more than seven percent (7%) over the fees in the immediately preceding term
What it means: Annual price can rise up to 7% without your consent at renewal. Below this cap, you have no ability to walk.
Negotiating position: Negotiate to 5% or lower. If spend is above $50k/yr, push for CPI-linked (typically 2-3% currently) instead of a fixed cap.

Typical wording: Customer commits to a 36-month term. Early termination fees equal to 100% of remaining fees shall apply.
What it means: You're locked in for 3 years with no exit except paying the full remaining balance.
Negotiating position: If product is unproven, negotiate 12-month term with vendor's standard uplift rate. If pricing discount is compelling, accept 24-month max with a one-time out at month 18.

Typical wording: Customer commits to annual spend of no less than $X. Any shortfall will be billed at the end of the term.
What it means: You pay for $X whether you use it or not. Overages are extra; under-usage is your problem.
Negotiating position: Negotiate a lower minimum with a true-up at midpoint, so you can adjust before paying for unused capacity.

Typical wording: Vendor may conduct quarterly reviews of actual usage. Any seats added will be billed at pro-rated list price and invoiced monthly thereafter.
What it means: Adding seats is easy (they'll invoice you). Removing seats before renewal is not an option.
Negotiating position: Add explicit downside-flexibility language: seats may be reduced at renewal; vendor shall right-size pricing to actual usage within 90 days.

Typical wording: Fees shall remain fixed for the duration of the initial term
What it means: Your rate stays level for 12 or 24 months regardless of vendor price list changes.
Negotiating position: This is good for you; make sure it survives any renewal negotiation. Ask vendor to extend fixed rate through the renewal period at same price.

Typical wording: All fees are due net thirty (30) days from invoice date. Late payments bear interest at 1.5% per month.
What it means: You have 30 days to pay. Late fees apply after that.
Negotiating position: For enterprise contracts, push for net-45 or net-60. For SMB contracts, net-30 is standard; focus energy elsewhere.

Typical wording: Each party shall indemnify the other against third-party claims arising from gross negligence or willful misconduct.
What it means: Both parties protect each other against lawsuits caused by egregious behavior.
Negotiating position: Standard. Read the carve-outs carefully: some vendors try to exclude IP indemnity for AI-generated content, data breach liability, or patent-troll claims.

Typical wording: Customer data shall be stored in data centers located in the United States.
What it means: Where your data physically lives. Matters for GDPR, Indian DPDP Act, and other data-sovereignty regulations.
Negotiating position: Required for EU operations: push for EU residency or mirroring. For India, ensure availability of a Mumbai/Chennai region if your buyer segment includes BFSI.

Typical wording: Vendor may suspend Customer's access to the Service in the event of non-payment for a period exceeding thirty (30) days.
What it means: Pay or lose access. Standard SaaS.
Negotiating position: Try to add a cure period: 'Vendor shall provide 10 business days written notice before suspension.' Protects against invoice disputes becoming service disruptions.

Typical wording: Vendor guarantees 99.9% uptime measured on a monthly basis. SLA credits equal to 10% of monthly fees for each full 1% below target.
What it means: 99.9% uptime = ~43 min of allowed downtime per month. Breach triggers small credits.
Negotiating position: For mission-critical systems, negotiate 99.95% or higher. Push for refund-not-credit remedies if downtime exceeds a hard threshold.

Typical wording: In the event of a Change of Control of Vendor, Customer may terminate this Agreement without penalty on 60 days written notice.
What it means: Lets you exit if vendor is acquired by someone you don't want to work with.
Negotiating position: Standard enterprise clause. SMB vendors often resist; push for it anyway, especially if you're in a regulated industry and worry about data moving jurisdiction after an acquisition.

Typical wording: Customer may, no more than once per year with 30 days notice, audit Vendor's usage reports for the purpose of verifying billing accuracy.
What it means: You can check their math. One audit per year
column5: Keep it. Rarely used but worth having. If vendor refuses, that's a signal to probe their billing practices harder.

Typical wording: Neither party shall be liable for failure to perform due to events beyond reasonable control including natural disasters acts of war and pandemics.
What it means: Nobody owes anybody if a catastrophe hits. Standard.
Negotiating position: Standard. Make sure it's bilateral and doesn't give vendor an escape hatch for routine outages they should have prevented.

Typical wording: Vendor shall provide upon request annual SOC 2 Type II reports, penetration test summaries, and current cyber-insurance certificates
What it means: You get proof of their security posture annually.
Negotiating position: Required for any enterprise relationship. If vendor doesn't have SOC 2 Type II and you're in finance / healthcare / government, keep looking.
